title: Fluctuational Quantum Electrodynamics of Dispersive Time-Varying Media
authors: Jaime E. Sustaeta-Osuna, Thomas F. Allard, Francisco J. García-Vidal, Paloma A. Huidobro
abstract: We present the theoretical framework of fluctuational quantum electrodynamics in frequency-dispersive and dissipative time-varying media. Our theory accounts for dispersion and losses in the temporal modulation, which is treated in an exact manner, without relying on perturbative methods. Thus, our work constitutes the first consistent quantization of the electromagnetic field in time-modulated material bodies. We derive a Fermi Golden Rule for time-varying media and use it to define the local density of states for these time-dependent systems, which includes both loss and gain contributions. Additionally, we prove the equivalence between the quantum Fermi Golden Rule and the power emitted by a classical harmonic point dipole. Moreover, we show that neglecting the dispersive and dissipative nature of the time modulation leads to erroneous predictions for both slow and fast modulations. Furthermore, we analyze the thermal radiation emitted by a time-varying material body, revealing new features in the enhancement of thermal emission in time-varying media. Finally, we study the dynamical Casimir effect, showing how the time modulation amplifies vacuum fluctuations and generates entangled pairs of polaritons exhibiting non-local spatial correlations.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive theoretical framework for Quantum Electrodynamics in dispersive, dissipative, and time-varying materials. It establishes a generalized fluctuation-dissipation theorem applicable to non-equilibrium systems by treating temporal modulation exactly. The results demonstrate that accurately modeling dispersion and losses is critical for predicting phenomena like enhanced thermal emission and the dynamical Casimir effect.
main_problem: Developing a rigorous theoretical framework for fluctuational quantum electrodynamics (QED) when applied to time-varying media that exhibit both frequency dispersion and dissipation.
main_result: The theory successfully derives a generalized Fermi Golden Rule applicable to non-equilibrium, time-modulated systems, showing that treating dispersion and losses exactly is crucial for accurate predictions of thermal emission and vacuum fluctuations.
method: The authors utilize Kubo's linear response theory extended to time-modulated media, employing the Green's dyadic formalism in the frequency domain to handle dispersive and dissipative effects non-perturbatively.
model_or_system: The system is a macroscopic dielectric body (e.g., SiC half-space) whose optical properties are modulated periodically in time. The theory models the interaction between the electromagnetic field and the material polarization density $P(r, t)$.
key_observables: Local Density of States (LDOS), spectral density of thermal radiation, correlation functions of the electric field, and entangled polariton pairs.
important_parameters: Modulation strength ($\alpha$), modulation frequency ($\Omega$), temperature ($T$), and material dispersion/loss parameters ($\epsilon(\omega)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes linearity for the media; key advancements overcome limitations of previous work that treated modulation perturbatively or assumed lossless behavior.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate spectral density vs. frequency comparisons, contrasting results from non-dispersive versus dispersive time modulation in a SiC half-space, and showing sideband structures related to phonon frequencies.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the generalized fluctuation-dissipation theorem for time-modulated systems (Chunk 1 & 2). It then applies this formalism to calculate the spectral density of thermal emission, explicitly comparing the necessity of including dispersion versus assuming non-dispersive modulation (Chunk 3). Finally, it analyzes the temperature dependence and low-temperature limit of these fluctuations (Chunk 4).
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it extends quantum electrodynamics into complex, realistic open quantum systems. The exact treatment of dispersion and dissipation in time-varying media provides powerful tools for understanding light-matter interaction dynamics beyond simple weak-coupling approximations.
